Notes: c. 28 BCE: Netzer, Kalman, Porat & Chachy-Laureys (JRA 2010) now date the start of building at Herodium c. 28 BCE (about 5 years before the 23 BCE they used to assume, following Kokkinos). On the NE slope, structures built with the early stairway, 'some of them perhaps even before it', include 'a small but well-equipped ritual bath carved as a cave into the bedrock'. This is Jewish ritual-purity practice at the site from its first building phase (Herod's court and building staff). No count.

c. 25/24-22 BCE (midpoint -23): D.R. Schwartz, 'Herodium in History' (Herodium Final Reports I, 2015), reads the chronology of Josephus, Ant. 15.323-325, as placing the main construction of Herodium in 25/24-22 BCE. Herodium was the only site Herod built explicitly in his own honour, commemorating his victory over 'the Jews'. Foundation of a royal palace-fortress; no figure for residents.

Herodian period, c. 23-20 BCE (approximate): Josephus, Ant. 15.325 (9.4): 'About the bottom there are habitations' supplied with water brought from far away; 'The plain that is about this citadel is full of edifices, not inferior to any city in largeness, and having the hill above it in the nature of a castle.' An ancient literary attestation of a built-up lower complex (Lower Herodium). Josephus does not say who lived there and gives no number; War 1.419-421 calls the whole complex 'a palace only'. Population blank.

c. 22-20 BCE (midpoint -21): Netzer et al. (JRA 2010) date the second phase of the 'tomb estate' at Lower Herodium to around these years. It included a 350 x 30 m funeral course, a monumental triclinium and 'a huge ritual bath'. An earlier U-shaped structure with an adjacent ritual bath was erased in this phase. Jewish ritual installations in the Herodian royal complex; no count of residents.

Herodian period (37-4 BCE; midpoint -20): Herodium Expedition, 'The Ritual Baths in the Palace-Fortress'. Two water installations inside the hilltop Palace-Fortress (a large double pool NW of the hall and a small stepped pool in the frigidarium of the bathhouse) 'appear to have been used as ritual baths during the original Herodian period'. Jewish ritual use within the royal palace; scale unknown.

4 BCE: Josephus, War 1.673 (33.9): Herod's body was carried from Jericho 200 furlongs 'to Herodium, where he had given order to be buried'. The army and 'five hundred of his domestic servants and freedmen' escorted it. These are a funeral procession, not residents, so Population is blank.

c. 6-58 CE (Agrippa I coins dated 41/2 CE): N. Ahipaz, coins from the tomb area (Herodium Final Reports I, 2015). Coins of the prefects (8), Agrippa I (9) and the procurators turn up mainly in Lower Herodium: 'it is possible that activity after the death of Herod the Great was concentrated in Lower Herodium. Activity at the site could have waned in the second half of the first century CE.' The author says explicitly: 'From the numismatic finds it is not possible to determine whether there was a Jewish settlement in Herodium prior to its conquest by the zealots.' Population blank.

1st century CE (midpoint 50): Josephus, War 3.55 (3.5) lists Herodium among the districts (toparchies) of Judea: '...and Idumea, and Engaddi, and Herodium, and Jericho'. As a district capital of Roman Judea, Herodium presumably had an administrative presence; Josephus gives no population figure.

66 CE: Netzer et al. (JRA 2010): Jewish rebels 'took over the site in A.D. 66 from the small, local Roman garrison'. Their presence is 'clearly attested' by layers of garbage and cooking ovens in and beside the debris of Herod's mausoleum, which they 'presume was deliberately destroyed by the Jewish rebels'. They also left Revolt coins, arrowheads and slingshots. The 'rebels who settled in the palace' were a rebel occupation of the fortress; no number is given.

c. 66-67 CE: D.R. Schwartz (2015): 'Herodium was occupied and garrisoned by rebels, probably early in the revolt'. By elimination and from the flow of Josephus's narrative, 'it seems that the fortress was in the hands of Idumeans' (so too Kasher), evidence of their assimilation into the Jewish people. Coin evidence shows the mausoleum was left intact for several years and destroyed only late in the revolt, possibly when more radical rebels joined. A rebel garrison of unknown size; Population blank.

66-71 CE (midpoint c. 68): Foerster's 1968-1969 excavations yielded 63 coins (abstract of the coin report in INR). The coins attest 'a period of decline after Herod's death' and 'a large-scale rebel habitation during the first Jewish revolt', followed by a 'short phase of Roman military presence after the revolt'. Rebel habitation; no count.

67/8-69/70 CE (year two of the revolt = 67/8, used as the year): N. Ahipaz (2015) counts First Revolt coins at Herodium: 29 in the mausoleum area (20 of year two, 4 of year three, 2 of year two/three, 3 of year four), 41 of years two-three from Corbo's dig in the Palace-Fortress, a hoard of 19 year-four coins from Foerster's dig, 34 from the tunnels, and only one in Lower Herodium. 'The rebels concentrated their activities in the area of the Mountain Palace-Fortress and on the slope, but they did not settle in Lower Herodium.' Coin counts are not population figures.

Pottery dated 66-132 CE: J. Gärtner, pottery from the mausoleum area (Herodium Final Reports I, 2015), Stage 4. It comes from activity 'during and after the First Jewish Revolt': tabun ovens, a refuse dump, and storage jars and 'especially cooking wares', with parallels at Masada and in Bar-Kokhba refuge caves. This is domestic (cooking and storage) evidence for the rebel occupants. The phase runs past 74 CE; the year 68 stands for its First Revolt part.

c. 66-71 CE (approximate): Herodium Expedition, 'Herodium during the period of the Great Jewish Revolt'. Zealots captured the site at the start of the revolt ('apparently in 66 CE'); it 'was occupied by Idumean Jews from Daroma (Idumea)' and apparently also by some zealots or Sicarii. 'The rebels crowded into the Fortress-Palace, exploiting every corner for their own day-to-day needs.' Possibly already during the revolt the Herodian hall 'was converted to a synagogue, with two ritual baths adjacent to it'. The expedition's ritual-baths page says these baths more likely date to the First than to the Second Revolt; the date of the synagogue conversion is debated. A rebel community with a synagogue and miqvaot; no count.

c. 66-70 CE (approximate): Eshel, Misgav & Porat, 'Legal Ostraca from Herodium' (abstract). The first publication of 'two small fragments of legal documents on sherds found at Herodium with estimated dating to the period of the Great Revolt'. The authors surmise they 'could have been brought to the site by refugees from the revolt'. Jewish legal documents of rebels or refugees; no count.

c. 68-69 CE (approximate; during Simon bar Giora's campaign in Idumea): Josephus, War 4.518 (9.5): Simon camped at Thecoe 'and sent Eleazar, one of his companions, to those that kept garrison at Herodium' to persuade them to surrender the fortress. The garrison refused (War 4.519; Eleazar was killed). This attests a Jewish rebel garrison holding Herodium; its size is not stated.

71 CE (some scholars say early 72): Josephus, War 7.163 (6.1): Lucilius Bassus, the new legate of Judea, 'took that citadel which was in Herodium, together with the garrison that was in it'. This is the Roman capture of the rebel fortress, the end of the Jewish rebel occupation. The fate of the garrison and its numbers are not stated. Population blank, because the source does not say that no Jews remained.

After 71 CE (c. 72): D.R. Schwartz (2015): after its fall 'Herodium seems to have remained in ruins and was basically abandoned. It is not clear whether a Roman garrison was stationed there, and there is virtually no evidence of anything else at Herodium for more than 60 years', until the Bar Kokhba revolt. Population is left blank rather than 0: the wording is hedged, and Gärtner's pottery report (same volume) speaks of continuous activity in the mausoleum area from the First Revolt to the Bar-Kokhba Revolt.
